systems.name: check.Linearizable
systems.title: Linearizability checker
systems.purpose: Decides whether a history matches a sequential model, within a step budget.
systems.what: `Linearizable` splits the history by the model's `Partition`, searches each partition for a real-time-respecting order that the model accepts, and combines the verdicts into one `Result`. The search is bounded in steps, not wall time, and reports Inconclusive when the bound is hit. On a violation it explains the longest order found and the operation it could not place.
systems.doc:
Linearizable checks whether history is linearizable with respect to the model: whether there is a total order of its operations that respects real time and in which each operation's output is what the model produces.

a precedes b in real time when a.Return < b.Call. Operations whose intervals touch or overlap may be ordered either way. An Unknown operation has no return, so it may be placed anywhere after its call, including after every other operation, which is how "it never happened" is expressed.

The search is the Wing & Gong algorithm with Lowe's memoization of (linearized set, state) pairs, the same one Knossos and porcupine use. It is exponential in the worst case, so partition the model where the object allows it.

interface.name: Linearizable
interface.signature: func Linearizable[S comparable, I, O any](m Model[S, I, O], history []Op[I, O], opts Options) Result
interface.doc: Checks a history against a model; returns a Result.

laws.text: On every history it decides within budget, its verdict equals that of trying every order of the operations.
Any history from running the operations one at a time, each inside its interval, is linearizable.
With a Partition function, the verdict is Pass exactly when every partition alone is.
The same history and options always give the same Result, Steps included.
Result.Err is nil exactly for Pass and wraps ErrInconclusive exactly for Inconclusive.
A Violation in any partition wins over Inconclusive in others.
laws.detail: Partitions are checked in sorted key order; the first violating partition is reported, else the first inconclusive one.

laws.text: Operations whose intervals merely touch may be ordered either way.
laws.detail: At equal times calls sort before returns, so a.Return == b.Call does not force a before b.

laws.text: MaxSteps bounds each partition separately; zero means 10 million.
laws.detail: Result.Steps is the total across partitions checked.

laws.text: An empty history, or empty partition, passes.
A Violation's Explanation names the operation that could not be placed.

assumes.text: Model.Step is pure and returns legal=true when known is false.
assumes.detail: The search memoizes (linearized set, state) and backtracks by restoring saved states.

assumes.text: Model states compare equal with == exactly when they are the same state.

systems.title: Sequential model
systems.purpose: Describes the sequential object a concurrent history must be equivalent to.
systems.what: A `Model` is a set of functions: `Init` for the starting state, `Step` to apply one operation and judge its output, an optional `Partition` to split histories into independent parts, and an optional `Describe` for reports. `Op` is the history entry the checker consumes. The model owns the object's semantics; the search is left to `Linearizable`.

systems.name: check.History
systems.title: History recorder
systems.purpose: Records client operations and their endings for Linearizable, timed by a World.
systems.what: `History` collects one `Op` per `Invoke`, and each returned `Call` is ended by `Return`, `Fail` or `Abandon`. Times are durations since the history was created, read from the World's clock. `Ops` produces the slice `Linearizable` consumes, leaving failed operations out and marking unfinished ones Unknown.
systems.doc:
History records client operations for Linearizable, with times from a World's clock. It is safe for concurrent use (the real World's clients run in parallel).

Each operation ends in one of three ways: - Return: the client saw the result. The output is known. - Fail: the client learned that it definitely did not happen (for example "not the leader, nothing was proposed"). It is left out of the history. - Abandon (a timeout), or no ending before the run ends: the outcome is unknown. It may still take effect later.

The first ending counts. A reply that arrives after Abandon is ignored, because the client has stopped waiting for it.

systems.name: main
systems.title: Bug-finding benchmark
systems.purpose: Measure how reliably simulation sweeps catch known, re-insertable bugs.
systems.what: dstbench is a command run from a target's directory. It reads `dstbench.json` (a `config`), which says where the sweeps live, which build tag compiles the bug switches in, which environment variable picks the bug, and which sweeps should catch each bug. For every (bug, sweep) cell, and for the bug-free baseline, it runs `go test` and turns the per-seed JSON records into a `cell` of statistics. It then prints a table and a summary, and can also write the cells to a JSON file. Running the tests and reading the per-seed records is left to `dsttest`, and so is grouping failures by signature.

It passes `-dst.keepgoing` and `-dst.json` pointing at a temporary JSONL file. It reads one `record` per seed run, sorts the records by index, and computes the failure rate with a Wilson 95% interval. It also computes the seeds and CPU time up to the first failure, how often the precondition was reached, the number of distinct failing roots and failure signatures, and failure splits per workload feature. Deciding whether a seed failed is left to the test run itself.

systems.name: dst
systems.title: World API
systems.purpose: Is what code uses, instead of the language and the standard library, for everything that waits or is nondeterministic: goroutines, channels, select, sleeping, the clock, timers, locks, contexts, randomness, files and the network.
systems.what:
A World provides them.

In production the World is real (package realworld): every operation is the plain Go one. In tests the World is simulated (package dsttest): one seed decides every goroutine interleaving, delay and fault, so a failing seed replays exactly.

Migrating code is a mechanical substitution:

go f()                  w.Go(f) make(chan T, n)         dst.MakeChan[T](w, n) c <- v / <-c / close    c.Send(v) / c.Recv() / c.Close() for v := range c        for v := range c.All() select { ... }          dst.Select(w, dst.OnRecv(c, ...), dst.OnSend(...), dst.Default(...)) time.Now / Sleep        w.Now() / w.Sleep(d) time.NewTimer/After     w.NewTimer(d) / w.After(d) sync.Mutex/WaitGroup    dst.Mutex / dst.WaitGroup (zero values work) sync.Cond               dst.Cond (dst.NewCond) context.WithTimeout     dst.WithTimeout(w, ctx, d) runtime.Gosched         w.Yield() math/rand               w.Rand() crypto/rand.Read        w.Rand().CryptoRead (crypto/rand.Reader: dst.CryptoReader(w)) os, net                 w.FS(), w.Net() os.Link                 dst.Link(w.FS(), old, new)

Inside a simulated World, code must not block any other way: a raw channel, sync.Mutex held across a wait, time.Sleep or real I/O escapes the scheduler. The simulator reports such escapes (it doesn't hang), and the dstlint analyzer finds them before running.

systems.purpose: Randomness that is seeded per machine in a simulation.
systems.what: `Rand` is the subset of `math/rand/v2`, plus `CryptoRead` standing in for `crypto/rand.Read`, plus `Stream` for named independent substreams. In a simulated World it wraps a generator the scheduler derives from a label, `machine/<name>/rand` for a machine and `<label>/<name>` for its streams. In the real World it uses the global generators, and `CryptoRead` uses `crypto/rand`. `CryptoReader` adapts a World's Rand to an `io.Reader` for libraries; crypto key generation still doesn't replay, so simulated machines need fixed keys.

A waiting send case panics if its channel is closed before it completes.
In a simulated World, Select2 and Select3 behave exactly as Select.
A simulated channel in a real-World select panics.
A send case on a receive-only Chan panics in the real World.

systems.name: dst.Mutex
systems.title: Mutex
systems.purpose: Is sync.Mutex for code that runs in a World.
systems.what: A zero-value `Mutex` wraps a `sync.Mutex`. In a simulation a contended `Lock` parks on the scheduler instead of blocking the baton, and `Unlock` wakes a parked waiter. The scheduler is cached per mutex, and a mutex belongs to one World.
systems.doc:
Mutex is sync.Mutex for code that runs in a World. The zero value is an unlocked mutex. In the real World it is a sync.Mutex; in a simulated World a contended Lock waits through the scheduler instead of blocking the baton.

In a simulated World, Lock (like RWMutex's Lock and RLock) is a scheduling point: another goroutine may run before it acquires, as in real Go, so races between separate critical sections are explored.

A Mutex (like every dst primitive) belongs to one World: don't share one between simulations running in parallel, or between a simulation and real code (a package-level mutex in code under test would be).

interface.name: Mutex.Lock
interface.doc: Acquire; waits through the scheduler in a simulation.

interface.name: Mutex.TryLock
interface.doc: Acquire if free, without waiting.

interface.name: Mutex.Unlock
interface.doc: Release and wake one waiter.

laws.text: Another goroutine may run before Lock acquires.
laws.detail: So a lost update across two locked sections is found.

laws.text: Unlock wakes one goroutine parked in Lock.
TryLock never waits or yields, even in a simulation.

systems.name: dst.RWMutex
systems.title: RWMutex
systems.purpose: sync.RWMutex for code that runs in a World.
systems.what: Wraps a `sync.RWMutex`. In a simulation, `Lock` and `RLock` yield and then retry `TryLock` or `TryRLock`, parking between attempts. A count of waiting writers keeps new readers out, so writers aren't starved. Unlocks wake every parked waiter so they can retry.

interface.name: RWMutex.Lock
interface.doc: Acquire for writing.

interface.name: RWMutex.Unlock
interface.doc: Release a write lock.

interface.name: RWMutex.RLock
interface.doc: Acquire for reading.

interface.name: RWMutex.RUnlock
interface.doc: Release a read lock.

laws.text: Once a writer waits in Lock, a new RLock waits until the writer has acquired.
In a simulation, Lock and RLock are scheduling points.
Unlock and RUnlock wake every parked Lock and RLock caller.

systems.name: dst.WaitGroup
systems.title: WaitGroup
systems.purpose: sync.WaitGroup for code that runs in a World.
systems.what: Keeps its own atomic counter next to a `sync.WaitGroup`. In a simulation, `Wait` parks on the scheduler until the counter reaches zero. `Go` counts a function and runs it in a new goroutine of the World.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Add
interface.doc: Add delta to the counter.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Done
interface.doc: Decrement the counter.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Go
interface.doc: Run fn in a counted World goroutine.

interface.name: WaitGroup.Wait
interface.doc: Wait until the counter is zero.

laws.text: Add that makes the counter negative panics.
Wait returns immediately when the counter is zero.
The Add that brings the counter to zero wakes every Wait caller.
Wait after Go(fn) returns only after fn has returned or panicked.

systems.name: dst.Once
systems.title: Once
systems.purpose: sync.Once whose second caller waits through the World.
systems.what: An atomic done flag plus a `dst.Mutex`. A concurrent second caller of `Do` waits on the mutex, which goes through the scheduler in a simulation, until the first caller's `f` has finished.

interface.name: Once.Do
interface.doc: Run f once across all callers.

laws.text: Do runs f at most once, however many goroutines call it.
A concurrent Do returns only after the first caller's f finished.
If f panics, later Do calls don't run f again.

systems.name: dst.Cond
systems.title: Cond
systems.purpose: sync.Cond for code that runs in a World.
systems.what: A condition variable over any `sync.Locker`, usually a `dst.Mutex`. Simulated waiters park on the scheduler, keyed by the `Cond`. The real World creates a `sync.Cond` lazily on the first real `Wait`. A waiter count lets `Signal` and `Broadcast` skip the scheduler when nobody waits.

interface.name: NewCond
interface.doc: Cond with locker l.

interface.name: Cond.Wait
interface.doc: Unlock L, wait for a wake, relock L.

interface.name: Cond.Signal
interface.doc: Wake one waiter.

interface.name: Cond.Broadcast
interface.doc: Wake all waiters.

laws.text: In a simulation, a Signal can't slip between Wait's unlock and its park.
laws.detail: No other simulated goroutine runs between Unlock and ParkOn.

laws.text: Wait holds L again when it returns.
Signal wakes one waiter; Broadcast wakes all.
A Signal or Broadcast with no waiters is lost.

systems.name: dst.Timer
systems.title: Timers
systems.purpose: time.Timer, AfterFunc and After by the World's clock.
systems.what: In a simulation a `Timer` is a scheduler event at a true time, computed from the duration on the arming machine's clock. When it fires it either sends the current time on a 1-buffered channel or spawns the `AfterFunc` goroutine. Timers armed by a machine that has since crashed don't fire. The real World wraps `time.Timer`.

interface.name: World.NewTimer
interface.doc: time.NewTimer.

interface.name: World.AfterFunc
interface.doc: Run fn in a new goroutine after d.

interface.name: World.After
interface.doc: time.After.

interface.name: Timer.Stop
interface.doc: Stop the timer.

interface.name: Timer.Reset
interface.doc: Rearm the timer for d.

laws.text: After Stop returns, no value from the stopped timer is received on C.
Stop returns true when the timer fired but its value wasn't received.
Reset reports whether the timer was active and rearms it for d.
A timer set on a machine that crashed since never fires.
AfterFunc runs fn in a new goroutine on the timer's machine.

systems.name: dst.Ticker
systems.title: Tickers
systems.purpose: time.Ticker by the World's clock.
systems.what: In a simulation a `Ticker` rearms itself after every tick and sends on a 1-buffered channel, dropping the tick if the receiver hasn't taken the previous one. The real World wraps `time.Ticker`.

interface.name: World.NewTicker
interface.doc: time.NewTicker.

interface.name: Ticker.Stop
interface.doc: Stop ticking.

interface.name: Ticker.Reset
interface.doc: Change the interval and restart.

laws.text: NewTicker with a non-positive interval panics.
A slow receiver sees at most one pending tick; extra ticks are dropped.
After Stop, no pending tick is received.
A ticker started on a machine that crashed since stops ticking.

systems.name: dst.WithCancel
systems.title: Contexts
systems.purpose: Cancellable and deadline contexts whose cancellation goes through the simulator.
systems.what: In a simulation, `WithCancel`, `WithTimeout` and `WithDeadline` return a `simCtx`. It is cancelled by a scheduler timer or by its parent, with no real timers and no goroutines. It is backed by a standard cancel context, so standard children are cancelled synchronously. `Done` and `AfterDone` let World code wait on or watch any context. The real World uses the `context` package directly.

interface.name: WithCancel
interface.doc: context.WithCancel for a World.

interface.name: WithTimeout
interface.signature: func WithTimeout(w *World, parent context.Context, d time.Duration) (context.Context, context.CancelFunc)
interface.doc: context.WithTimeout by the World's clock.

interface.name: WithDeadline
interface.signature: func WithDeadline(w *World, parent context.Context, deadline time.Time) (context.Context, context.CancelFunc)
interface.doc: context.WithDeadline by the World's clock.

interface.name: Done
interface.doc: A Chan closed when ctx is done.

interface.name: AfterDone
interface.signature: func AfterDone(ctx context.Context, f func()) (stop func() bool)
interface.doc: Run f once ctx is done; returns stop.

laws.text: Calling a cancel func again, or after the deadline, changes nothing; the first error stays.
Cancelling a context cancels its dst children synchronously, in creation order.
WithDeadline at or before now returns a context already DeadlineExceeded.
WithDeadline later than the parent's deadline keeps the parent's deadline.
Deriving from a cancelled parent yields a context cancelled with the parent's error and cause.
In a simulation, deriving from, waiting on or watching a non-dst cancellable context panics.
laws.detail: Contexts that are never done, and standard cancel contexts below a dst one, are accepted.

laws.text: AfterDone on a done dst context runs f at once and stop reports false.

systems.name: dst.Inject
systems.title: Fault points
systems.purpose: Named fault points and BUGGIFY points that a simulation decides per seed.
systems.what: `Inject` asks the scheduler's fault-point registry what happens to one call of a named service operation: `None`, `Fail` or `FailAfter`, possibly with added latency. `Call` wraps a call to an outside service in that decision. It maps the two faults to the caller-visible errors given in `Errors`, and lets the caller's context cut injected latency short. `Do` is `Call` for an operation that returns only an error, with no context. `Buggify` asks whether an unusual code path should be taken. With no registry, as in the real World, nothing is ever injected.

interface.name: Inject
interface.doc: Decide the Fault for one call of a named point.

interface.name: Call
interface.signature: func Call[T any](ctx context.Context, w *World, name string, errs Errors, op func() (T, error)) (T, error)
interface.doc: Run op behind a fault point, honouring ctx.

interface.name: Errors
interface.doc: Errors Call returns for Fail and FailAfter.

interface.name: Do
interface.signature: func Do(w *World, name string, op func() error) error
interface.doc: Run an error-only op behind a fault point.

interface.name: World.Buggify
interface.doc: Whether a named BUGGIFY point fires.

interface.name: ErrInjected
interface.doc: Default error for an injected fault.

laws.text: A nil Before or After in Errors makes Call return ErrInjected.
laws.detail: So Do, which passes an empty Errors, returns ErrInjected on both Fail and FailAfter.

laws.text: In a simulation, Call with an already-done ctx returns ctx.Err() without running op.
laws.detail: The request is never sent. This only applies when a fault-point registry is present.

laws.text: On None with no cut-short latency, Call returns op's result unchanged.
Inject sleeps injected latency on the World's clock before returning, ignoring any context.
Without a fault-point registry, Inject returns None and Call returns op() regardless of ctx.

assumes.text: The registry decides faults per seed, only during the fault phase.
A quiet Inject leaves every other decision of the seed unchanged.
A Buggify point is active in about a quarter of seeds, firing on about a quarter of calls.

systems.name: dst.LockFile
systems.title: File locks
systems.purpose: Exclusive, non-waiting advisory file locks on a World's filesystem.
systems.what: `LockFile` is flock(2) with LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB over a World `FS`: the lock file a database keeps in its directory. It delegates to the filesystem's `Locker` implementation, which both the real World's (on unix) and the simulated disk provide. A held lock is reported as `ErrLocked`; filesystems without locks are reported as unsupported.
systems.doc: LockFile takes an exclusive advisory lock on name in fsys, creating the file if it doesn't exist, without waiting: if anyone holds it, LockFile returns ErrLocked. It is flock(2) with LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB, the lock file databases keep in their directory (LevelDB's LOCK, rosedb's FLOCK): a second LockFile of the same file fails even from the same process, and the lock lasts until unlock is called or the process dies (a crash or a kill releases it; the file stays). A filesystem that isn't a Locker returns errors.ErrUnsupported.

interface.name: LockFile
interface.signature: func LockFile(fsys FS, name string) (unlock func() error, err error)
interface.doc: Lock name in fsys without waiting; returns unlock.

laws.text: While a lock is held, LockFile of the same file fails with ErrLocked; after unlock it succeeds (both Worlds: the FS contract suite).
A crash or a kill of the holder's machine releases its locks; nothing else does (simulated disk).
LockFile on a filesystem that isn't a Locker returns an error wrapping errors.ErrUnsupported.
laws.detail: It takes no lock and creates no file in that case.

laws.text: ErrLocked matches syscall.EWOULDBLOCK under errors.Is.
laws.detail: So code written against flock(2)'s error keeps working.

assumes.text: The filesystem's Locker.LockFile implements the flock semantics LockFile documents.
assumes.detail: LockFile only forwards to it; exclusivity, file creation and release on crash come from the FS.

change.reason: Only line numbers moved after the new import; behaviour unchanged.

systems.name: dst.World.Yield
systems.title: Yield
systems.purpose: Lets other goroutines run, as runtime.Gosched does.
systems.what: `Yield` is the World's `runtime.Gosched`, for code that waits on another goroutine with no World operation in between, such as a spin on an atomic. In the real World it is `runtime.Gosched`. In a simulated World it asks the scheduler to run someone else, so the awaited goroutine runs, time advances, or the spin is reported as a deadlock.

laws.text: In a simulated World, Yield returns only after another goroutine has taken a step or time has advanced; a spin waiting for a sleeping goroutine ends at its wake-up after a handful of iterations, and a spin no one can end is a deadlock.

assumes.text: The scheduler's YieldToOthers returns only after another task stepped or time advanced.
assumes.detail: Yield's simulated behaviour, including deadlock reports, is entirely the scheduler's.

change.reason: New System: World.Yield was added.

systems.name: dst.Current
systems.title: Current World
systems.purpose: The calling goroutine's World, for leaf code no World reaches.
systems.what: `Current` looks up the scheduler task running the caller and returns the World recorded on that task's machine when the World was built. Any goroutine the simulator doesn't run gets one shared real World. It is a last resort that dstlint reports; the determinism check catches goroutines that unknowingly get the real World during a simulation.
systems.doc:
Current returns the World of the calling goroutine, for code that no World can reach. It is a last resort: pass a World (as a field, a parameter, an option) wherever one is reachable, and use Current only in leaf code with no owner to hand it one, such as a package-level helper called from everywhere. dstlint reports every use.

For a goroutine a simulated World started, Current is that machine's World. For any other goroutine (one a raw go statement started, a finalizer, the test's own goroutine) it is the real World, even while a simulation runs: such a goroutine gets real randomness and the real clock, and nothing reports it. The determinism check is the backstop: a seed whose runs differ because of it is reported as nondeterministic. Outside a simulation the World Current returns has goroutines, time, locks and randomness but no filesystem or network (realworld.New gives those).

interface.name: Current
interface.doc: The World of the calling goroutine.

laws.text: A goroutine a simulated World started gets its own machine's World (even with other machines and other simulations running at once); a goroutine no World started gets the real World.
Outside a simulation, Current's World has no filesystem or network: FS and Net panic.
laws.detail: It is built with only real randomness; realworld.New gives a World with files and network.

laws.text: Every call from a goroutine no World started returns the same real World.

assumes.text: sched.CurrentTask returns the task running the calling goroutine, or nil for any other goroutine.

change.reason: New System: Current was added.

systems.name: dst.Link
systems.title: Hard links
systems.purpose: os.Link over a World filesystem, for checkpoints and ingestion.
systems.what: `Link` makes a second name for a file on a World `FS`, as storage engines do for checkpoints. It forwards to the filesystem's `Linker` implementation, which the real World's and the simulated disk provide; the simulated disk models the new name as a directory change for crashes. Filesystems without hard links are reported as unsupported.
systems.doc: Link is os.Link on fsys: it makes newname a second name (a hard link) for the file oldname, as checkpoints and ingestion in storage engines do. The data is one file, the same through either name, and it lasts while either name does. The new name is a directory change: like a create, it survives a crash only once its directory is synced. Linking a directory, or onto a name that exists, fails. A filesystem that isn't a Linker returns errors.ErrUnsupported.

interface.name: Link
interface.signature: func Link(fsys FS, oldname, newname string) error
interface.doc: Make newname a hard link to oldname in fsys.

laws.text: After Link, a write through either name reads through the other, removing one name keeps the data under the other, and linking onto an existing name or a directory fails (both Worlds: the FS contract suite).
After a crash, a link survives only as the directory rules allow: lost unless its directory was synced, never with data the file's own rules would have lost (simulated disk: the crash model).
Link on a filesystem that isn't a Linker returns an *os.LinkError wrapping errors.ErrUnsupported.
laws.detail: The error names Op "link" and both names, as os.Link's does; nothing is linked.

assumes.text: The filesystem's Linker.Link implements os.Link semantics and the crash rules Link documents.
assumes.detail: Link only forwards to it.

change.reason: New System: Link and Linker were added.

systems.name: dstgrpc
systems.title: gRPC over World
systems.purpose: Runs gRPC services and clients in a World.
systems.what:
Your generated code and service implementations stay unchanged:

s := dstgrpc.NewServer(w)              // instead of grpc.NewServer() pb.RegisterFooServer(s, impl)          // unchanged go s.Serve(ln)                         // ln from w.Net().Listen

conn, _ := dstgrpc.NewClient(w, "db-1:50051") // instead of grpc.NewClient client := pb.NewFooClient(conn)               // unchanged

In the real World these are grpc-go's server and client. In a simulated World, Server implements grpc.ServiceRegistrar and the client implements grpc.ClientConnInterface over the World's network with a compact framing (one connection per call), so faults, latency and deadlines follow the seed and the World's clock. Unary and streaming calls, metadata (headers and trailers), status codes and interceptors are supported; status details are not carried.

interface.name: Server.RegisterService
interface.doc: Registers generated service descriptors (grpc.ServiceRegistrar).

interface.name: Server.Serve
interface.doc: Accepts and serves calls on a World listener.

interface.name: Server.Stop
interface.doc: Closes the listeners.

interface.name: ClientConn
interface.doc: grpc.ClientConnInterface plus Close, for generated clients.

laws.text: The same generated code and implementation work in both Worlds: unary and streaming calls, status codes, metadata.
A call's deadline reaches the server's context and ends the call with DeadlineExceeded, even if the server never answers.
Unary and stream interceptors wrap every call, on both sides.
Interceptors installed by several options run in option order, the first outermost.
laws.detail: This matches grpc-go's Chain*Interceptor, so the order is the same in both Worlds.

laws.text: In a simulated World, a failed call returns only a status code and message, never status details.
Real*Options take effect only in the real World; a simulated World ignores them.

assumes.text: Messages passed to calls are proto.Message values.
assumes.detail: In a simulated World, any other type fails the call.

systems.name: dstgrpc.Server
systems.title: Simulated server
systems.purpose: Serves registered gRPC services over World listeners, one connection per call.
systems.what: Holds the registered service descriptors and, in a simulated World, accepts connections and runs each call in its own World goroutine. Each call reads a call header (method, timeout, metadata), builds a context bounded by the World's clock, sends the request to the generated handler through the interceptors, and writes back a header, any reply messages and a trailer with the status. Headers and trailers set through grpc.SetHeader, SendHeader and SetTrailer reach the client.

interface.name: NewServer
interface.doc: Server for a World with interceptors installed.

interface.name: Server.RegisterService
interface.doc: Registers a generated service implementation.

interface.name: Server.Serve
interface.doc: Accept loop; returns the listener's Accept error.

interface.name: Server.Stop
interface.doc: Closes every listener passed to Serve.

laws.text: A call to an unregistered service or method fails with Unimplemented.
A client hanging up during a unary call cancels the handler's context.
laws.detail: After the request is decoded, a watcher reads the connection and cancels the context on error or EOF.

laws.text: A stream's RecvMsg returns io.EOF after CloseSend, and Canceled if the client went away.
SetHeader after the header has been sent returns an error.
laws.detail: The header is sent by the first SendMsg, by SendHeader, or when the handler returns.

laws.text: Trailer metadata set by the handler is delivered even when the call fails.
After Stop, Serve returns the listener's error.

assumes.text: Closing a dst listener makes a pending Accept return an error.

systems.name: dstgrpc.ClientConn
systems.title: Simulated client
systems.purpose: Makes unary and streaming gRPC calls over the World's network.
systems.what: `NewClient` returns grpc-go's client in the real World. In a simulated World it returns a client that dials the target once per call. The call header carries the method, the time left before the context's deadline (measured on the World's clock) and the outgoing metadata. The client maps transport failures to gRPC status codes and fills Header and Trailer call options from what the server sent.

interface.name: NewClient
interface.signature: func NewClient(w *dst.World, target string, opts ...DialOption) (ClientConn, error)
interface.doc: Client for a target, with interceptors installed.

interface.name: ClientConn
interface.doc: Invoke, NewStream and Close for generated clients.

laws.text: A unary Invoke fails with Internal unless the server sends exactly one response message.
Failing to reach the target returns Unavailable, or DeadlineExceeded/Canceled if the context ended.
Ending the call's context stops a blocked call, even if the server is silent.
laws.detail: AfterDone sets an already-passed deadline on the connection, so pending reads and writes fail.

laws.text: grpc.Header and grpc.Trailer call options are filled once Invoke returns or a stream ends.
Stream SendMsg returns io.EOF on a broken connection; RecvMsg returns the real status.
Header on a call that ended with no header returns the call's error status.
laws.detail: Messages that arrive before the header are queued for RecvMsg, not lost.

assumes.text: dst.AfterDone runs its function when the context ends and its stop function prevents that.

systems.name: dstgrpc.framer
systems.title: Wire framing
systems.purpose: Encodes calls as typed, length-prefixed frames on one connection.
systems.what: Each frame is a type byte, a 4-byte big-endian length and a payload. The types are call header, message and close-send from the client, and header and trailer from the server. Metadata and strings are length-prefixed, and messages are encoded with deterministic protobuf marshalling, so a seed always produces the same bytes on the wire.

laws.text: The same messages and metadata always encode to identical bytes.
laws.detail: Metadata keys are sorted and proto marshalling is deterministic, so map order never reaches the network.

laws.text: A truncated metadata or string payload decodes to a short-frame error, never a panic.

assumes.text: World connections deliver written bytes in order, without duplication.

systems.name: dsthttp
systems.title: HTTP over World
systems.purpose: Runs net/http code in a World: your http.Handlers and http.Client calls stay unchanged; only how the server is started and which transport the client uses come from here.
systems.what:
go dsthttp.Serve(w, ln, mux)                          // instead of http.Serve(ln, mux) client := &http.Client{Transport: dsthttp.Transport(w)} // instead of http.DefaultClient

In the real World these are http.Serve and http.DefaultTransport. In a simulated World, the server is a small loop that parses requests with http.ReadRequest and calls the handler, and the transport dials through the World's network, one connection per request.

In simulated code, bound requests with a context (dst.WithTimeout), not http.Client.Timeout, which uses real timers.

laws.text: The same handlers and client calls work in both Worlds (status, headers, bodies, keep-alive, methods).
A request ends with the context's error when the context ends.
laws.detail: That holds even if the server never answers.

laws.text: A panic in a handler fails the simulated run (unlike net/http, which logs it), except http.ErrAbortHandler.

assumes.text: In the real World, http.Serve and http.DefaultTransport give the same handler-visible behaviour.
assumes.detail: In the real World, dsthttp passes straight through to net/http and adds no behaviour of its own.

change.reason: Only the doc-comment wording of the verified law client-honours-context changed; the meaning is the same. Line numbers after it moved up by one.

systems.name: dsthttp.Serve
systems.title: Simulated server
systems.purpose: Accepts World connections and serves buffered HTTP/1.1 responses from a handler.
systems.what: In a simulated World, `Serve` accepts connections and starts a named World goroutine for each one. Each goroutine reads requests one after another with `http.ReadRequest`. Each request runs the handler with a World-cancellable context. The handler writes into an in-memory `responseWriter`, and the whole response is sent once the handler returns. Streaming is therefore not supported: `Flush` does nothing.

interface.name: Serve
interface.signature: func Serve(w *dst.World, ln net.Listener, h http.Handler) error
interface.doc: Accepts and serves connections until the listener's Accept fails.

laws.text: Serve returns the listener's Accept error.
laws.detail: Closing the listener is how a caller stops Serve.

laws.text: The client sees no response bytes until the handler returns, even after Flush.
The first WriteHeader status wins; later WriteHeader calls are ignored.
laws.detail: Write without WriteHeader sets 200. A handler that writes nothing gets 200.

laws.text: A non-empty body without Content-Type gets a sniffed Content-Type.
The handler's request context is cancelled as soon as the handler returns.
A handler panicking with http.ErrAbortHandler closes the connection without sending a response.
The connection closes after a response if the request or response asks for Close.
laws.detail: Otherwise the server drains any unread request body and reads the next request on the same connection.

assumes.text: dst.WithCancel contexts are cancelled through the World, deterministically.

systems.name: dsthttp.Transport
systems.title: Simulated transport
systems.purpose: Sends each request over a new World network connection.
systems.what: In a simulated World, `Transport` returns a RoundTripper. For each request it dials the World's network, writes the request with Connection: close, and reads one response. The request context controls the connection through deadlines: the context's deadline becomes the connection's deadline, and cancellation sets a deadline in the past. That unblocks any pending I/O. Only plain http URLs are supported.

interface.name: Transport
interface.doc: Returns the World's RoundTripper.

interface.name: Client
interface.doc: Returns an http.Client using Transport(w).

laws.text: A request whose URL scheme isn't http fails without dialing.
A URL host without a port dials port 80.
Every request uses its own connection and is sent with Connection: close.
Closing the response body closes the connection.
A body read that fails after context cancellation returns the context's error.
laws.detail: io.EOF passes through unchanged even if the context has already ended.

assumes.text: World Net().DialContext stops dialing when the context ends.
Setting a past deadline on a World connection makes pending reads and writes fail.
dst.AfterDone runs its callback when the context ends, unless stop was called first.

systems.name: dstlint
systems.title: Simulation linter
systems.purpose: Is an analyzer that finds code in simulated packages that would escape the World: raw goroutines, channels, select, the clock, sync primitives that wait, context timers, global randomness, and the os, net, net/http and gRPC entry points.
systems.what:
A package opts in with a comment in any of its files:

//dst:simulated

Every use of dst.Current (the calling goroutine's World) is reported in every package, opted in or not: it is a last resort, for leaf code that no World can reach. Excuse each use with //dst:ok and the reason.

A line can be excused with a comment on it or the line above:

mu.Lock() //dst:ok guards a cache no goroutine waits on

Run it with `go run github.com/prince776/go-dst-kit/dstlint/cmd/dstlint ./...` or as a go vet tool.

interface.name: Analyzer
interface.doc: go/analysis analyzer reporting World escapes and dst.Current uses.

laws.text: Every construct in the escape list is reported, with its World replacement, in an opted-in package.
Packages without //dst:simulated aren't reported, except for dst.Current.
Every use of dst.Current is reported, in every package: it is the last resort for code no World reaches.
A //dst:ok comment on or above a line suppresses its report.
Only the function Current declared in the dst package is reported as dst.Current.
laws.detail: The match uses the declaring package path `github.com/prince776/go-dst-kit/dst` and requires a `*types.Func`. A user function or variable named `Current` in another package is never reported by this check.

laws.text: Only an exact //dst:simulated line comment opts the package in.

A //dst:ok comment excuses only its own line and the line below it.

laws.text: A report names a standard-library package by its full path, such as crypto/rand.

systems.name: main
systems.title: Migration command
systems.purpose: Rewrites a Go package in place so it runs in a dst.World.
systems.what: dstmigrate loads packages with type information and does the mechanical part of adopting go-dst-kit. It rewrites channels, select, time, sync, go statements, runtime.Gosched, math/rand and crypto/rand, contexts and os file I/O into the World's equivalents. With -map it also redirects a project's own functions and methods to replacements that take the World. Then it formats the file and fixes its imports. It works in two passes: an AST rewrite (`migrator`) that needs the original types, then a text pass (`spliceSelects`) that turns each select into `dst.Select` plus a switch. It leaves whatever it can't map to a person: places with no World in scope get the placeholder `__w`, and calls with no World equivalent are reported on stderr.

systems.name: main.migrator
systems.title: AST rewrite
systems.purpose: Rewrites one file's syntax to World calls using the original type information.
systems.what: A `migrator` walks each declaration twice. The first walk rewrites statements and calls while the original types are still valid: sends, receives, range, close/len/cap, nil channels (in returns, assignments, comparisons, call arguments and composite literals), go statements, wg.Go on a sync.WaitGroup, runtime.Gosched, time, rand, crypto/rand, context, file calls and -map calls. It also records a `selectPlan` for each select. The second walk rewrites types and a few selectors: chan T, *os.File, the sync types and sync.NewCond, *time.Timer and *time.Ticker, and crypto/rand.Reader. It counts changes so the caller knows whether a file changed, and it reports unmappable constructs once each on stderr.

interface.name: migrator.file
interface.doc: Rewrites a file in place; reports whether anything changed.

laws.text: A rewritten file always imports dst.
Channel nil returns, assignments and comparisons become the zero dst.Chan.
laws.detail: The zero value is parenthesized so it stays valid in if and for conditions.

laws.text: nil passed to a channel parameter or used as a channel literal element becomes the zero dst.Chan.
laws.detail: This covers variadic channel parameters, except when the call spreads with `...`, and struct fields (keyed or positional), slice, array and map elements. Conversions and builtins are left alone.

laws.text: Generated element types spell nested channel types as dst.Chan.
laws.detail: A chan of chans, or a slice, array, map or pointer containing a channel, is written as the rewritten declarations spell it, in zero values and select plans.

laws.text: v = <-c becomes v, _ = c.Recv(); a receive inside an expression becomes dstRecv(c).
Select-case communications are left to the select pass, never rewritten as plain sends or receives.
wg.Go(f) on a sync.WaitGroup becomes wg.Go(w, f).
sync.NewCond(l) becomes dst.NewCond(l).
runtime.Gosched() becomes w.Yield().
Intn, Int63 and Int63n become IntN, Int64 and Int64N on w.Rand().
rand.N(d) becomes T(w.Rand().Int64N(int64(d))), with T the call's result type.
Other rand functions, except New*, are warned about and left drawing from the global generator.
crypto/rand.Read becomes w.Rand().CryptoRead; crypto/rand.Reader becomes dst.CryptoReader(w).
laws.detail: Reader is matched by its package path, so this works under any import name.

laws.text: context.With*Cause becomes the dst variant without its cause argument, with a warning.
The same warning at the same position is printed only once.

change.reason: Adds rewrites for wg.Go, sync.NewCond, runtime.Gosched and -map calls, and spells nested channel element types as dst.Chan.

A channel returned by a function or method of another package, or held in a field of another package's type, stays a raw channel, and a warning says that waiting on it can't be simulated. A context's Done() also counts as foreign: in a select it becomes dst.OnDone, and everywhere else it stays raw.

ctx.Done() is never converted and never warned about.

systems.name: main.migrator.goStmt
systems.title: Go statements
systems.purpose: Turns go statements into w.Go and keeps go's argument-evaluation timing.
systems.what: `go f(a, b)` evaluates f's receiver and the arguments right away, but a closure passed to w.Go would evaluate them later. goStmt therefore binds each non-trivial receiver and argument to a fresh `goArgN` variable before calling w.Go. A `go func(){...}()` with no arguments is passed to w.Go directly.

laws.text: A variadic spread f(xs...) keeps its spread in the goroutine's call.

systems.title: File I/O rewrite
systems.purpose: Maps os and ioutil file calls and *os.File methods to the World's FS.
systems.what: Package-level os functions that the World's FS has as methods become `w.FS().Name(...)`. Open, Create, ReadFile, WriteFile and Link become dst helpers that take the FS first. File names pass through unchanged, so they must be relative to the FS root. Calls with no World equivalent, and *os.File methods that dst.File lacks, are left alone and reported.

interface.name: migrator.fileMethod

os.Link becomes the dst.Link helper taking the FS first.

systems.name: main.spliceSelects
systems.title: Select splicing
systems.purpose: Rewrites each select as text into dst.Select plus a switch over the original case bodies.
systems.what: Selects are rewritten after formatting, as text, so their case bodies are copied verbatim, comments included. Each select becomes a block that declares `selN` and the received-value variables, calls `dst.Select(world, ...)` with one callback per case that records which case fired, and then switches on `selN` to run the original body of that case. It needs a `selectPlan` per select, made by the AST pass from the original types: the World expression and each case's element type.

interface.name: spliceSelects
interface.signature: func spliceSelects(name string, src []byte, plans []selectPlan) ([]byte, error)
interface.doc: Rewrites the file's selects, given one plan per select in source order.

interface.name: selectPlan
interface.doc: World and per-case element types for one select.

laws.text: Case bodies run after dst.Select returns, so break, continue and return keep their meaning.
If the number of selects found differs from the plans, an error is returned.
laws.detail: The caller sorts plans into source order first, because they are made innermost first.

laws.text: v, ok := <-c in a case keeps its = or := token and both variables in that case's body.
case <-ctx.Done() becomes dst.OnDone(ctx, ...).
A send case names its element type only when the value's type differs from it.
The generated switch's default panics, so a select whose cases all terminate still terminates.

assumes.text: dst.Select runs exactly one case callback before it returns.

systems.name: main.setPos
systems.title: Generated positions
systems.purpose: Gives generated nodes positions so the printer keeps comments in place.
systems.what: Generated syntax has no positions. setPos fills the unset positions of a generated node with the position of the node it replaces, so the printer doesn't move nearby comments into it. zeroPos (setPos with NoPos) clears every position in a parsed expression so it is laid out fresh. Two positions carry meaning and are never touched: a call's Ellipsis and a declaration's parentheses.

interface.name: setPos
interface.doc: Sets every unset position in a node to p.

interface.name: parseExpr
interface.doc: Parses an expression with all positions cleared.

A call's Ellipsis is never changed, so f(xs...) and f(xs) stay distinct.
A GenDecl's parentheses are never changed, so var (...) prints as it did.

systems.name: main.migrator.mapCall
systems.title: Call mapping
systems.purpose: Redirects -map'd functions and methods to replacements taking the World first.
systems.what: With -map, a project can name its own wrappers (a clock, say) and the functions that replace them. Keys are importpath.Func for functions and (importpath.Type).Method for methods. A method matches its key whether its receiver is T or *T.
Only selector calls are mapped; a bare f() inside f's own package is not.
A mapped call is not rewritten by any other call rule.
A target in the migrated package is called unqualified; any other target's package is imported.

systems.name: dsttest
systems.title: DST runner
systems.purpose: Runs deterministic simulation tests: it sweeps seeds, and for each one builds a simulated World of machines, injects faults, checks invariants, and reports failures with a command that replays them exactly.
systems.what:
func TestStore(t *testing.T) { dsttest.Run(t, dsttest.Options{Seeds: 500, Faults: dsttest.AllFaults}, func(h *dsttest.Harness) { for _, name := range []string{"db1", "db2", "db3"} { h.Machine(name, func(w *dst.World) { store.Serve(w, name) }) } h.Go(func(w *dst.World) { workload(w, h) })     // clients, on a machine that never fails h.Always("one leader", checkLeaders)            // after every step h.Final("converged", checkConverged)            // after recovery }) }

The setup function runs once per seed, possibly in parallel with other seeds: keep every piece of state the run uses inside it.

Each seed runs in phases. During the fault phase the runner crashes and restarts machines, pauses them, partitions the network and lets disks lose unsynced data, at rates chosen per seed (swarm testing: some seeds turn whole fault classes off). During the recovery phase every machine is back and the network is whole: a correct system must recover. Then the Final checks run. A failing seed prints:

go test -run '^TestStore$' -dst.seed=2891 -dst.v

which reruns exactly that seed with an event log.

Flags: -dst.seed=N (one seed), -dst.seeds=N, -dst.first=N|random (where the sweep starts; nightly runs use random), -dst.v (event log), -dst.parallel=N.

laws.text: A failing seed fails again, identically, when replayed.
Code whose behaviour isn't decided by the seed is reported as nondeterministic, with the step where runs diverge.
An Always invariant that breaks at any step fails the seed at that step.
After the fault phase, every machine is running and the network is whole until the run ends.
A sweep fails if an Expect-ed behaviour never happened in any seed.
Known-bad systems (a WAL without fsync, a pool that deadlocks) fail within the default number of seeds.
Workload goroutines still running when recovery ends fail the seed.
laws.detail: That covers h.Go goroutines and those they started; the report names what each waits for, and Final checks run only after the workload is done.

laws.text: Unfinished workload is reported as slow if it finishes during one more fault-free recovery phase, else stuck.
The runner never crashes a NeverCrash machine.
-dst.first=random starts each sweep from a new seed, and -dst.first=N from N.
Machine clocks stay within the Clock bounds; fast, slow and at-bound clocks all occur.
With Pause faults the runner pauses machines and resumes every one by the recovery phase.
Fault points fail and Buggify points fire only during the fault phase, and never with Faults.Points and Faults.Services off.
With Services faults the runner takes whole services down: every point of the service fails together.
Turning on pauses, outages, fault points or losses leaves the times of each seed's crashes and partitions as they were.

With Gray faults, across seeds: slow links, lossy links losing segments, connections reset at a heal, slow machines stalling, and slow disks all occur; none of the stalls, losses or resets happen after the fault phase.

A machine's Downtime and Pauses, and a pair's Cut, are exactly the crashes and kills to their restarts, the pauses to their resumes (or the crash that ended them), and the blocks to their heal, at the true times they happened; no machine runs inside one of its Down or Pause intervals.

In about a third of the Gray seeds (Swarm.MildGray), only one or two of the gray kinds that would be on (slow links, lossy links, resets at heal, slow machines, slow disks, UDP blackholes) stay on, and the rest are off; every other field, and every field of the other seeds, is what the seed draws without it.

With Disk, about two thirds of the seeds draw a chance (Swarm.DiskHoleProb) that a crash writes a file back out of order, page by page; without Disk it is zero; every other field is what the seed draws without it.
With Gray faults, across seeds, lossy links lose datagrams and some links drop all UDP while TCP flows; neither happens after the fault phase, nor without Gray.
A lost machine never boots again, even when a restart was already scheduled; the runner loses only machines the test's OnLoss accepts at that moment, and reports each loss once.
laws.detail: With Faults.Loss and no OnLoss, the seed fails.

laws.text: A machine restarted from a workload goroutine doesn't count as that goroutine's work.
Turning Kill on changes which crashes keep the page cache, not when crashes happen or to which machine; Kill alone only kills; and a killed machine finds everything it wrote.

With OnPanic, a panic it accepts kills only its machine's process (its other goroutines stop; its disk keeps the page cache) and the machine restarts; a panic it rejects, any panic without OnPanic, and any panic on a NeverCrash machine fails the run.

assumes.text: The scheduler replays a run exactly given the same seed, forks and code.
assumes.detail: Every replay, determinism and corpus guarantee here builds on this.

change.reason: New package laws [gray-mild] and [disk-holes]: Swarm gains MildGray and DiskHoleProb, and disks can write files back out of order on a crash.

systems.what: The per-run object passed to the test's setup function. Newer draws (mild gray, disk holes) come from their own random streams so older fields keep their values. The swarm feeds the disk, network and nemesis.

systems.name: dsttest.runPath
systems.title: One run

Then comes a fault-free recovery phase: network and disk faults stop, every partition heals, and every machine is resumed and restarted. After that run the unfinished-workload check and the Final checks. It returns a `Result` with the error, fingerprint, checkpoints, coverage and fork information.

systems.name: dsttest.Harness.nemesis
systems.title: Nemesis
systems.purpose: Injects the swarm's faults on a schedule until the fault phase ends.

Every fault except a fill and a loss schedules its own undo (restart, heal, resume, service back); full disks stay full until recovery stops disk faults. It stops when the fault phase's simulated time runs out.

laws.text: No nemesis event due after the fault phase ends ever runs.
Every nemesis partition splits the machines and test into two non-empty sides.
Each nemesis crash or kill schedules that machine's restart.
NeverCrash machines can still be paused and partitioned by the nemesis.
The nemesis never loses a NeverCrash machine.
The nemesis fills each disk at most once, never a NeverCrash or lost machine's.

interface.doc: Lists stuck and slow workload goroutines.

systems.title: Run paths
systems.purpose: Names a run as a root seed plus forks, with a text form.

interface.name: Path

interface.name: Fork

interface.doc: The path with one more fork.

interface.doc: The path's text form.

interface.name: ParsePath
interface.doc: Parse a path's text form.

Then leaves the original path's forks unchanged.
A path without forks replays with -dst.seed, otherwise with -dst.path.

systems.name: dsttest.Report
systems.title: Sweeps and reports
systems.purpose: Runs many paths and aggregates their results into one report.
systems.what: A `Report` gathers every run's results, the failing ones, determinism divergences, summed coverage and Expect-ed behaviours never reached. It is produced by `Sweep`, over consecutive seeds, or by `Explore`, over guided forks. Both run paths in parallel through `runAll`, which reruns some paths to check determinism and stops early on failure unless `KeepGoing`.

interface.name: Report
interface.doc: A sweep's results, failures, divergences and coverage.

interface.name: Report.OK
interface.doc: No failures, divergences or unreached expectations.

interface.name: Divergence
interface.doc: A path whose two runs differed.

laws.text: Report.OK is true exactly when Failed, Nondeterministic and NeverHappened are empty.
Without KeepGoing, no new run starts after one fails; unrun paths are omitted.
Every failing run is run twice to check determinism.
A report with failures lists no NeverHappened behaviours.
Report.Coverage sums each behaviour's counts over every run.

systems.name: dsttest.Sweep
systems.title: Seed sweep
systems.purpose: Runs consecutive seeds and reports them.
systems.what: Runs `Options.Seeds` seeds starting at `FirstSeed` (both overridable by flags), checking the first `DeterminismChecks` of them for determinism, and aggregates the results in seed order.

interface.name: Sweep
interface.signature: func Sweep(opts Options, setup func(h *Harness)) Report
interface.doc: Run the seeds and return the report.

The first DeterminismChecks seeds each run twice; -1 checks none but failures.
With no Seeds set, a sweep runs 100 seeds, or 10 with -short.

systems.name: dsttest.Explore
systems.title: Guided exploration
systems.purpose: Spends runs forking from where earlier runs did something rare.
systems.what: Runs in generations of `ExploreBatch`. Each path is either a fresh consecutive seed or a fork of an earlier run at a rare feature (a marker, a marker order, or an interleaving pair), drawn with weight inversely proportional to how many runs reached it. Choices depend only on earlier generations' results, so an exploration replays from its options alone.

interface.name: Explore
interface.signature: func Explore(opts Options, setup func(h *Harness)) Report
interface.doc: Guided runs; report as Sweep does, in run order.

laws.text: Explore's paths depend on its options alone, not on Parallel.
laws.detail: Each generation is chosen only from earlier generations, with a fixed batch size and an rng seeded by FirstSeed.

laws.text: Explore runs Options.Explore runs, or Options.Seeds if that is not positive.
No feature is forked from more than ExploreBudget times.
No explored path has more than 8 forks.
Fresh seeds are consecutive from FirstSeed, and the first generation is all fresh.

systems.name: dsttest.Run
systems.title: Test entry
systems.purpose: Runs a sweep or one path inside a Go test and reports failures.
systems.what: `Run` is what tests call. With `-dst.seed` or `-dst.path` it runs one path, optionally with an event log. Otherwise it replays the saved corpus, sweeps or explores, optionally saves failures, replays the first result and first failure in a fresh process of the test binary, writes `-dst.json` records, and fails the test with a replay command per failing seed, each divergence and each unreached expectation.

interface.name: Run
interface.signature: func Run(t testing.TB, opts Options, setup func(h *Harness)) Report
interface.doc: Sweep, explore or replay one path as a test.

laws.text: With -dst.seed or -dst.path, Run runs that one path and fails t if it fails.
Run lists at most three failing seeds unless KeepGoing.
Run fails the test if a seed's trace or outcome differs in a new process.
laws.detail: Checked for the first result and the first failure, unless DeterminismChecks is -1 or -dst.xprocess=false.

laws.text: Each printed replay command names the top-level test and the path's flag.
-dst.json appends one line per run, with its trace in hex.

systems.name: dsttest.replayCorpus
systems.title: Failure corpus
systems.purpose: Saves failing paths and replays them before each sweep.
systems.what: The corpus is a directory of JSON entries, one per saved failing path, under `testdata/dst/<test>/<subtest>` by default. Each entry stores the path, why it was kept, the date and the trace, so a replay can tell an exact replay from a drifted one. `Run` replays the corpus first; with `-dst.save` it saves new failures and refreshes drifted entries.

laws.text: A corpus entry that fails on replay fails the test, exact or drifted.
A passing corpus entry is only logged, never a failure.
With -dst.save, drifted entries get the current trace but keep their Kept reason.
Saving writes at most three failures and never overwrites an existing entry.
Entries replay in sorted file order; a path always maps to the same file.

systems.name: dsttest.Signature
systems.title: Failure signatures
systems.purpose: Reduces a failure to its kind, so one bug's seeds group together.
systems.what: `Signature` takes the first line of an error and blanks out what varies between runs of one bug: numbers and durations and long hex become N, and quoted values after the first ": " become Q, while the check's own quoted name before it stays.

interface.name: Signature
interface.doc: A failure's normalised first line.

laws.text: Signature(nil) is the empty string.
Only the error's first line affects its Signature.
Errors that differ only in numbers or long hex have the same Signature.
Quoted text before the first ": " stays; quoted text after becomes Q.

systems.name: dedupe
systems.title: Exactly-once dedupe
systems.purpose: Is exactly-once processing over at-least-once delivery: a producer retries each message until it is acknowledged, and a consumer applies each message once however often it arrives, across its own crashes.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, a mutex, TCP, files) written against a dst.World.

The consumer keeps one write-ahead log of applied message IDs: applying a message and remembering that it was applied are the same durable record, so no crash can separate them.

Bugs plants known mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

interface.name: Consumer.Apply
interface.doc: Applies a message ID unless it was already applied.

interface.name: Consumer.Serve
interface.doc: Accepts producers; acknowledges each line's ID once applied.

interface.name: EffectsLog
interface.doc: File name of the log of applied IDs.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant known consumer mistakes.

interface.name: Sender
interface.doc: Producer that learns a per-address attempt timeout.

interface.name: Sender.Deliver
interface.doc: Sends an ID until acknowledged, retrying with backoff.

laws.text: Every message the producer delivers is applied exactly once, under crashes, partitions, resets and power loss.
Once faults stop, every message is acknowledged.
The wire protocol is one ID per line, answered with "ok <id>".
laws.detail: Both the producer and the consumer rely on this framing. An ID that contains a newline cannot be delivered.

change.reason: The package function Deliver is replaced by the Sender type and its Sender.Deliver method, which adapts the attempt timeout per address. The producer child is now dedupe.Sender.

systems.name: dedupe.Consumer
systems.title: Consumer
systems.purpose: Applies each message ID once, durably, and acknowledges it over TCP.
systems.what: The consumer owns the `EffectsLog` write-ahead log. Each record in it is an applied message ID, and an in-memory seen set is rebuilt from that log when the consumer starts. `Apply` takes a mutex, skips IDs already seen, and otherwise appends the ID to the log before marking it seen. `Serve` handles producer connections, one goroutine per connection, and acknowledges each ID only after it has been applied. Durability itself is left to the `wal` package.

interface.name: NewConsumer
interface.doc: Opens EffectsLog and rebuilds the seen set from it.

interface.name: Consumer.Apply
interface.doc: Applies a message ID unless it was already applied.

interface.name: Consumer.Serve
interface.doc: Serves producers on a listener until Accept fails.

interface.name: EffectsLog
interface.doc: File name of the log of applied IDs, in order.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant known consumer mistakes.

laws.text: Apply of an already-applied ID returns nil and appends nothing.
After NewConsumer, every ID recorded in EffectsLog counts as already applied.
laws.detail: This holds with no Bugs set: the seen set is rebuilt from the effects records themselves.

laws.text: EffectsLog holds applied IDs in apply order, each at most once.
Apply that returns an error leaves the ID unapplied in memory, so a retry may apply it.
Serve sends "ok <id>" only after Apply of that ID returned nil.
laws.detail: If Apply fails, the connection is closed without an acknowledgement, so the producer retries.

laws.text: Serve returns only when Accept fails, returning that error.

assumes.text: wal.Log.Append returns only after the record is durable.
wal.Open recovers every record whose Append succeeded, in append order.
dst.Mutex gives mutual exclusion among World goroutines.

systems.name: dedupe.Sender
systems.title: Producer
systems.purpose: Delivers message IDs at least once, adapting each address's attempt timeout.
systems.what: `Sender` is the at-least-once side. Each attempt dials the consumer, sends the ID as one line and waits for the matching "ok <id>" reply, all within the attempt's timeout. Failed attempts are retried after an exponential backoff with random jitter, and each failure doubles the attempt timeout. The timeout that finally worked, cut by a quarter, is remembered for that address so the next message starts from it. Time and randomness come from the World, and removing duplicates is left to the consumer.

interface.name: Sender
interface.doc: Producer holding learned per-address timeouts; zero value usable.

interface.name: Sender.Deliver
interface.doc: Sends an ID until acknowledged, retrying with backoff.

laws.text: Sender.Deliver returns only after reading exactly "ok <id>" for its own ID.
laws.detail: A reply for some other ID, or any read error, counts as a failed attempt.

laws.text: Each attempt, including dial, write and read, ends within its timeout of World time.
The first attempt to a new address uses a 300ms timeout.
laws.detail: No attempt timeout is ever below 300ms.

laws.text: After each failed attempt the next attempt's timeout doubles, capped at 5s.
After success, the next Deliver to that address starts at three quarters of the successful timeout.
laws.detail: The starting timeout never drops below 300ms. Timeouts are tracked per address, so other addresses are not affected.

laws.text: Retry waits start at 10ms, double each time, and are capped at 1s, plus jitter.
laws.detail: The jitter is random and less than the current backoff, so a single wait is under 2s.

laws.text: A Sender delivers one message at a time; concurrent Deliver calls are unsupported.
laws.detail: The per-address timeout map has no lock.

assumes.text: dst.WithTimeout and connection deadlines expire in World time.
w.Rand and w.Sleep are deterministic under the simulated World.

change.reason: New System that replaces dedupe.Deliver. Delivery is now Sender.Deliver, and the fixed 300ms attempt timeout is replaced by one learned per address: it doubles on failure up to 5s and shrinks by a quarter after success, never below 300ms.

systems.name: gcounter
systems.title: Grow-only counter
systems.purpose: Is a replicated grow-only counter (a G-Counter CRDT): any node accepts increments, nodes gossip their state, and once gossip gets through every node reports the same total.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, TCP, files) written against a dst.World.

Each node counts its own increments in one slot of a vector and persists the vector before acknowledging, by the classic atomic file replace: write a temporary file, fsync it, rename it over the old one, fsync the directory. Merging takes the larger count per slot, so gossip can repeat, reorder and duplicate freely.

Bugs plants known mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

interface.name: Node.Serve
interface.doc: Answers inc, get and merge requests on a listener.

interface.name: Node.Gossip
interface.doc: Pushes state to random peers forever, backing off slow peers.

interface.name: Node.Value
interface.doc: Sum of the counts this node knows.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that plant known mistakes in a node.

laws.text: Once faults stop, every node reports the same value.
The value lies between the acknowledged and the attempted increments.
laws.detail: That holds under crashes, partitions, resets and power loss.

laws.text: Zero-valued Bugs gives the correct replica; each set field plants one mistake.
laws.detail: Tests rely on the default being correct and each switch being independent.

systems.name: gcounter.Node
systems.title: Replica
systems.purpose: One replica: durable local counts, max-merge of gossip, request server.
systems.what: A `Node` holds a vector of counts keyed by node name. The vector is guarded by a `dst.Mutex` that is never held across disk I/O, and a second mutex makes increments write the state file one at a time. An increment bumps its own slot, snapshots the vector and persists it before it is acknowledged: write a temp file, fsync it, rename it into place, fsync the directory. If that write fails, the count stays and the request gets no reply. Incoming gossip is merged by taking the per-slot maximum. `Gossip` regularly sends the whole vector to a random peer, with a per-peer timeout that grows while the peer keeps failing. `Start` rebuilds the vector from the state file on restart.

interface.name: Start
interface.signature: func Start(w *dst.World, name string, peers []string, bugs Bugs) (*Node, error)
interface.doc: Recovers a replica from the World's disk.

interface.name: Node.Serve
interface.doc: Answers inc, get and merge requests on a listener.

interface.name: Node.Gossip
interface.doc: Pushes state to random peers forever, backing off slow peers.

interface.name: Node.Value
interface.doc: Sum of the counts this node knows.

laws.text: An inc request is answered "ok" only after the new state is renamed into place and the directory synced.
An increment whose persist fails keeps its count locally but gets no reply.
laws.detail: A failed increment is never decremented, because gossip may already have spread it. Rolling it back would let the next increment reuse a count that peers hold, and that increment would be lost. An unacknowledged increment may or may not count.

laws.text: A node's Value never decreases while it runs.
laws.detail: Increments only add to the node's own slot, failed persists included. Merges never lower a slot.

laws.text: Value, merges and gossip never wait on an increment's disk writes.
laws.detail: The counts mutex is released before persist, so only other increments queue behind a slow disk.

laws.text: Concurrent increments write the state file one at a time, in count order.
laws.detail: Each snapshot is taken under persistMu, so a later write never carries a lower own count than an earlier acknowledged one.

laws.text: Merging the same state again, or older state, does not change Value.
laws.detail: Merge takes the per-slot maximum, so it is idempotent and commutative and never lowers a slot.

laws.text: Gossip to a failing peer doubles its timeout, capped at 2s; success resets it to 200ms.
laws.detail: The doc comment says up to 5s, but the code caps it at 2s because one slow peer stalls the whole gossip loop.

laws.text: Start with no state file yields a node whose Value is zero.
Start on an unparseable state file returns a corrupt-state error, not a node.
Malformed merge payloads and unknown commands get no reply and change nothing.
Serve returns the listener's Accept error and otherwise never returns.

assumes.text: The World's FS Rename atomically replaces the state file.
File Sync then dst.SyncDir make the renamed state survive power loss.
Gossip is started only on nodes with at least one peer.
assumes.detail: Picking a peer from an empty list panics.

change.reason: Side effect changed: a failed persist used to undo the increment locally, and now the count is kept. The law about undoing failed increments now says the count is kept, and a new law adds that Value never decreases. Evidence lines after the edit moved up by 2.

systems.name: gcounter.call
systems.title: Client calls
systems.purpose: One-request-per-connection client for the replica's text protocol.
systems.what: `callWithin` dials a node through the World's network, sends one line and reads one reply line, all under a World-timed deadline; `call` uses the default 200ms `timeout`. `Inc` uses the default and `Get` takes the wait from its caller. Anything short of the expected reply is reported as failure, which for `Inc` means the increment's fate is unknown.

interface.name: Inc
interface.doc: Asks a node to increment; true means counted.

interface.name: Get
interface.signature: func Get(w *dst.World, addr string, d time.Duration) (uint64, error)
interface.doc: Asks a node for its value, waiting at most d.

laws.text: Inc returns true only when the node replied exactly "ok".
laws.detail: False means the increment may or may not have been counted.

laws.text: Inc gives up after 200ms of World time; Get gives up after d.
laws.detail: The deadline covers dial, write and read together.

laws.text: Get returns an error when there is no reply or it is not a number.

systems.name: heartbeat
systems.title: Heartbeat detector
systems.purpose: Is a failure detector over UDP: workers send heartbeats to a monitor, which suspects a worker it hasn't heard from for Timeout.
systems.what:
A worker can also leave for good, and says so in its heartbeats.

UDP loses, duplicates and reorders datagrams, so each heartbeat carries a sequence number, and the monitor ignores any not newer than the last it accepted. The sequence number starts with the worker's incarnation, kept on disk and bumped at every boot, so a restarted worker's heartbeats are newer than its old ones. The monitor knows the members from its configuration, not from who it has heard: after it restarts, a worker that is down is still suspected.

interface.name: Interval
interface.doc: How often a worker sends a heartbeat.

interface.name: Timeout
interface.doc: Silence after which the monitor suspects a worker.

interface.name: Status
interface.doc: A worker's self-reported status: Active or Leaving.

interface.name: Bugs
interface.doc: Switches that inject classic detector mistakes.

interface.name: Worker.Run
interface.doc: Sends heartbeats every Interval, optionally leaving after leaveAt.

interface.name: Worker.Leave
interface.doc: Records leaving on disk, then announces it.

interface.name: Worker.Status
interface.doc: The worker's own status.

interface.name: Monitor.Serve
interface.doc: Reads and applies heartbeats from a packet conn.

interface.name: Monitor.Suspected
interface.doc: Whether a member has been silent past Timeout.

interface.name: Monitor.Status
interface.doc: Monitor's view of a worker's status.

laws.text: Once the monitor has seen a worker leave, it never sees it active again, under loss, duplication, reordering, crashes, pauses and partitions.
A worker that has been down for Timeout plus the network's worst delay is suspected by a monitor that has been up that long.
Once faults stop, every live worker is trusted, with its latest status.
After a worker restarts, its first heartbeat is accepted by the monitor.
laws.detail: The incarnation is bumped and saved before sending, and it occupies the top 32 bits of the sequence, so it beats every sequence from earlier boots.

inspect.name: Worker.OnSend
inspect.doc: Hook for each heartbeat's sequence and status before it is sent.

inspect.name: Monitor.OnStatus
inspect.doc: Hook for changes in the monitor's view of a status.

systems.name: heartbeat.Worker
systems.title: Worker
systems.purpose: Sends sequenced heartbeats and keeps its incarnation and departure on disk.
systems.what: A `Worker` keeps a small state file holding its incarnation and whether it has left. Every boot bumps the incarnation. Each heartbeat carries the sequence `inc<<32 | n` and the worker's status. Leaving is permanent: it is saved to disk before it is announced, and it survives restarts. Disk errors while loading or saving state are retried every 10ms until they succeed, rewriting the temp file from scratch each time, so `NewWorker` and `Leave` wait out a full or failing disk rather than panicking.

interface.name: NewWorker
interface.signature: func NewWorker(w *dst.World, name, monitor string, bugs Bugs) *Worker
interface.doc: Loads state, bumps incarnation durably, returns the worker.

interface.name: Worker.Run
interface.doc: Heartbeats every Interval; leaves once leaveAt has passed.

interface.name: Worker.Leave
interface.doc: Persists leaving and sends a Leaving heartbeat.

interface.name: Worker.Status
interface.doc: Active, or Leaving once it has left.

laws.text: A worker that ever called Leave boots as Leaving after a restart.
Leave saves the departure to disk before sending the Leaving heartbeat.
laws.detail: A crash cannot leave a sent Leaving heartbeat with an Active worker after restart. If the save fails, Leave keeps retrying and sends nothing until it succeeds.

laws.text: Leave on a worker that is already Leaving writes and sends nothing.
Sequence numbers strictly increase across a worker's sends, restarts included.
laws.detail: Holds while fewer than 2^32 heartbeats are sent per boot. The NoIncarnation bug breaks it.

laws.text: NewWorker saves the bumped incarnation before any heartbeat is sent.
NewWorker and Leave retry disk errors until success; they never panic or skip saving.
laws.detail: Each failed load or save is retried after a 10ms World sleep. The whole temp file is rewritten each time, because after a failed fsync nothing is known about state.tmp. A missing state file isn't an error: it means incarnation 0, not left.

laws.text: Run returns only when opening the UDP socket fails, with that error.

assumes.text: dst FS rename plus SyncDir makes the state file replacement atomic and durable.
dst FS disk faults are temporary, so retrying eventually succeeds.
assumes.detail: A permanent fault would block NewWorker or Leave forever.

inspect.name: Worker.OnSend
inspect.doc: Called with sequence and status before each send.

change.reason: A disk error in NewWorker or Leave used to panic. Now both retry every 10ms until the load or save succeeds, so they can block, and they rely on disk faults being temporary.

systems.name: heartbeat.Monitor
systems.title: Monitor
systems.purpose: Applies the newest heartbeat per member and judges suspicion by silence.
systems.what: A `Monitor` has a fixed member set taken from its configuration. For each member it records the last accepted sequence number, the status, and when it last heard from it. It accepts a heartbeat only if the sequence is newer, and suspects a member after `Timeout` of silence, counting from its own boot if it has never heard from that member. All state is guarded by a `dst.Mutex`, so `Serve` can run alongside `Suspected` and `Status`.

interface.name: NewMonitor
interface.doc: Monitor over configured workers, with boot time set to now.

interface.name: Monitor.Serve
interface.doc: Applies datagrams until a read error, then returns it.

interface.name: Monitor.Suspected

systems.name: lease
systems.title: Lease service
systems.purpose: Is a lock service with leases: a server grants one client at a time the right to act for a limited time, and clients renew it.
systems.what:
Ordinary Go (goroutines, TCP, timers) written against a dst.World.

Safety rests on time: a client may act only until its lease ends, and the server grants the lease to someone else only after it ended. Both sides must measure conservatively:

- the client counts its lease from when it sent the request (the server granted it later, so it expires later there); - the client shortens its lease by the protocol's drift bound, since its clock may run slower than the server's; - durations, not timestamps, cross the network: clocks disagree; - a client that can't renew stops acting when its lease ends; - a restarted server, which forgot its grants, waits one lease length before granting anything.

Bugs plants the classic mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

Holders' writes are fenced: each grant carries a token that grows, and the store rejects a token lower than one it has seen, so a holder that paused past its lease (a GC pause, a VM stall) can't overwrite the next holder's work.

systems.name: twophase
systems.title: Two-phase commit
systems.purpose: Is two-phase commit: a coordinator moves money between accounts held by two participants, atomically, despite crashes of any of them and a network that loses, delays and partitions.
