Ordinary Go (goroutines, a mutex, TCP, files) written against a dst.World.

Each participant holds one account. A transfer is a transaction with a delta for each participant. The coordinator logs "begin", asks both to prepare, logs its decision, and tells them. A participant that votes yes has first logged the prepared delta, so it can still commit after a crash; while in doubt it holds its lock and asks the coordinator. A restarted coordinator aborts every transaction it began but didn't decide (presumed abort).

systems.name: wal
systems.title: Write-ahead log
systems.purpose: Is a write-ahead log: an append-only file of checksummed records that survives crashes.
systems.what:
It is ordinary Go written against a dst.World's filesystem, and an example of what deterministic simulation finds in storage code.

A record is a 4-byte length, a 4-byte CRC-32 of the length and the data, and the data. The checksum covers the length so that zeros (a file whose size reached the disk before its data did) never read as a valid record: the CRC-32 of empty data is 0. Append returns only once the record is durable. Open recovers: it reads records until the first incomplete or corrupt one (a write torn by a crash), truncates the file there, and continues after it.

When Append fails (a full disk writes part of the record; a failed fsync leaves it readable but never durable, though the next fsync succeeds), the log truncates the file back to the end of its last durable record before appending again: appending after the failed bytes would leave garbage, or a hole, before records acknowledged later.

Bugs plants known mistakes; the test shows the simulator catches each.

systems.name: sched.Scheduler
systems.title: Baton scheduling
systems.purpose: Runs tasks one at a time in a seed-decided order and reports failures.
systems.what: The `Scheduler` owns the task list, the runnable set and the baton. `Run` loops: apply a due `Fork`, pick an eligible runnable task (uniformly or by PCT priority), hand it the baton, and wait for it to hand back at its next `Yield`, `YieldToOthers`, `Park` or exit, then run the `AfterStep` invariant. A task in `YieldToOthers` is parked as a spinner until some other task takes a real step or a timer fires, so busy-wait loops let others run, let time advance, and end as a deadlock when nothing else can happen. Failures (panic, misuse, deadlock, watchdog, limits, invariant errors) are recorded once and returned from `Run`. The exception is a task panic that the optional `OnPanic` hook calls fail-stop: that kills the task's machine instead of failing the run. It also gives out seeded randomness per label, keeps a fingerprint of the run, and can record interleaving pairs for an explorer.

systems.name: simfs
systems.title: Simulated disk
systems.purpose: Is a simulated disk for one machine: an in-memory filesystem with os semantics, behind a page cache that a crash empties the way real kernels and disks may.
systems.what:
It is adversarial but legal. Live operations behave exactly like os (the contract suite runs against both). What survives a crash is anything POSIX and real journaling filesystems allow, chosen by the seed:

- Data written to a file is durable only after the file's Sync. - Directory changes (create, mkdir, link, rename, remove) form one ordered journal: a crash keeps a prefix of the unsynced ones, and a Sync of a directory makes the journal durable up to that directory's last change. A rename is atomic. - By default each file's unsynced writes survive independently of other files' (as on ext4 data=writeback or XFS), and a file's Sync covers its own data only. With Ordered, everything is one queue in issue order and any Sync commits everything before it, like a journal commit on ext4's default data=ordered. - The first lost write of a file may survive in part (torn). - With HoleProb, in harsh mode, a file's unsynced writes may instead reach the disk out of order, page by page: after a crash each page they touched holds either its last written content or what was durable, independently of the other pages, and the file's size is either the durable one or the last written one (so a size past the data written reads as zeros, and a page not written back shows the file's older content, as in a reused file). Files with an unsynced truncate keep the prefix rule. - Power can fail inside a Write, Sync or directory operation. - Open files go stale after a crash. - A kill (the process dies, the host stays up) keeps the page cache: every completed write and directory change is still there after restart, and still unsynced.

Disk errors, as Linux reports them (Options' error rates, and Fill):

- A full disk (Fill) stays full: from then on, until StopFaults, the disk holds no more bytes than it did. A write that doesn't fit writes what does and fails with ENOSPC (as os.File does after a short write); creating a file or directory fails with ENOSPC while no byte is free; removing or truncating files frees space under the cap. Nothing already written is lost. (Space is freed at Remove, even while the file is open.) - A Sync of a file with unsynced writes may fail with EIO, and then those writes will never be durable: they stay readable until a crash, which loses them, and the next Sync succeeds (Linux marks the pages clean after a writeback error and reports the error once: PostgreSQL's "fsyncgate"). Retrying the Sync doesn't help; only rewriting the data does. Directory Syncs don't fail. - A Write or Read may fail with EIO, doing nothing.

Not modelled: a failed fsync's pages being evicted (so reads return the old data), bit rot, misdirected writes.

After a crash, the disk is in a state the rules above allow, in either mode.
Every state the rules allow happens for some seed.
Data covered by a completed Sync, and names covered by a completed directory Sync, survive every crash.
Hole decisions draw only from a stream of their own: a disk whose hole draws all come out "no" crashes exactly as a disk without holes, so turning holes on leaves every other draw as it was.
After a kill, every completed write and directory change is visible, and none became durable: a later power loss may still lose any of it.

After Fill, nothing grows the disk past what it held: a write writes exactly the bytes that fit and fails with ENOSPC, creates fail with ENOSPC while no byte is free, removing or truncating frees space that can be written again, nothing written before is lost, and StopFaults lifts the cap.

A Sync that fails with EIO makes exactly that file's unsynced writes non-durable for good (still readable until a crash, gone after it, though a later Sync succeeds); other files' writes are unaffected.
A Write or Read that fails with EIO transfers no bytes and moves no offset.
A New disk's root directory exists and survives every crash.
laws.detail: The root is created directly and is never a pending entry, so no crash can remove it.

laws.text: The same seed and the same calls give the same crash outcome.
laws.detail: All fault choices, including handle directory order, injected errors and holes, come from per-machine seeded streams. Iteration over maps is sorted.

laws.text: With all error rates zero, enabling error injection draws nothing from the seed.
laws.detail: A zero probability returns before drawing, so seeds without errors keep the schedule they had before errors existed.

laws.text: File times are the machine's local clock, offset from 2030-01-01 UTC.

With `HoleProb` (outside Ordered mode), a file may instead be written back page by page, using a separate holes stream and `PageSize` pages. Everything else is discarded and the live tree is reset to the durable one. `Options` set how adversarial this is, and `StopFaults` turns the faults off.

systems.name: simnet
systems.title: Simulated network
systems.purpose: Is a simulated network between machines: TCP-like connections with seeded latency, partitions and resets, implementing net.Listener and net.Conn so code written against the net package runs on it.
systems.what:
Its model of TCP:

- Bytes on a connection arrive in order, exactly once, each write after a seeded latency. - A partition stalls a connection (like TCP retransmitting): nothing crosses it, and after Heal everything held arrives, in order. - A crashed machine is silent (power loss sends nothing): its peers' reads wait, until their deadlines or until the machine restarts and answers their next packet with a reset. - A killed process's host stays up, and its kernel closes the process's sockets: what was written is still delivered, then a FIN (peers read EOF at once); data sent to it afterwards draws a reset; dials to its ports are refused until it listens again. - Data sent to a closed connection is answered with a reset, which arrives after anything sent before it and discards what the receiver hasn't read yet (so closing with unread input can destroy a response in flight, as RFC 7230 §6.6 warns). - Dialing an address with no listener is refused; dialing across a partition waits for Heal or the deadline. - ResetProb resets connections at random, as middleboxes and kernels do. - Links (Options.Links) are each direction between two hosts, with their own behaviour drawn once per seed: a slow link adds latency to every write; a lossy link loses segments, which TCP retransmits, so a loss delays the stream by a retransmission timeout (200ms, doubling while losses repeat, at most 3.2s) and nothing is lost or reordered. - HealResetProb: at Heal, a connection that crossed the partition is reset with this chance (a NAT, firewall or load balancer that forgot the connection answers its next packet with a reset), else it carries on with what was held.

Addresses are "machine:port"; "localhost" is the dialing machine. A machine named by an IP literal in canonical form ("10.0.0.1") has the net package's address types: *net.TCPAddr for listeners and connections, *net.UDPAddr for sockets and datagrams' sources, so code that type-asserts them works; other names are host:port names.

With HealResetProb, connections that crossed a partition may be reset at Heal (both ends fail); connections that didn't cross never are; with 0, none is.
Nothing crosses a partition; after Heal, everything held arrives in order.

A killed process's peers read what it wrote, then EOF, at once; their next write is reset; dials to it are refused.

laws.text: Data sent to a closed connection resets it, and the reset discards what the other end hasn't read.

Each link is drawn once: it may be slow (extra latency on every write and datagram), lossy (segments retransmitted, datagrams gone), or blocking UDP while TCP still flows.

systems.name: worldhook

systems.purpose: Lets World implementations build a *dst.World without a public dst constructor.
systems.what: Package worldhook is a back door between dst and the packages that build Worlds (realworld and the simulator). Values come back as `any` to avoid an import cycle; building the World itself is left to dst.

laws.detail: A non-nil Sched means a simulated World driven by that scheduler, with Epoch as simulated time zero.

systems.name: worldtest
systems.title: World contract suite
systems.purpose: One set of checks every World, real or simulated, must pass.
systems.what: worldtest holds the contract suite for `dst.World`. The same checks run against the production World and the simulated one, so the two behave alike. A check is a named function that takes a fresh World and fails by panicking with a `Failure`. The suite comes in three lists. The core list covers concurrency, select, time, sync, context and rand. The other two cover the filesystem (advisory file locks and hard links included) and the network (TCP and UDP). Running the checks on each World is left to the test files that import the package.

interface.name: Check
interface.doc: A named contract check run against one World.

interface.name: Failure
interface.doc: Panic value a failing check raises.

interface.name: Checks
interface.doc: Channel, select, time, sync, Cond, context and rand checks.

interface.name: FSChecks
interface.doc: Filesystem, file-lock and hard-link checks on an empty FS.

interface.name: NetChecks
interface.doc: TCP and UDP checks against w.Net() of a fresh World.

laws.text: A failing check panics with a Failure, never another value.
laws.detail: Every failure goes through `failf`, so a runner can tell a contract failure from a crash.

laws.text: A check fails only in the goroutine that runs Check.Fn.
laws.detail: Goroutines a check starts with w.Go never call failf. They report back through a Chan or shared state, or just return, so a failure shows up the same way in both Worlds.

laws.text: A check uses only the World it is given, so it runs unchanged on either World.
laws.detail: Waiting, time, goroutines, randomness and I/O all go through `w` or dst helpers. The checks never use real time or the real OS.

laws.text: Check names are unique and say which area they test.
laws.detail: Each name starts with its area: `chan/`, `select/`, `select2/`, `select3/`, `time/`, `sync/`, `context/`, `rand/`, `fs/`, `net/` or `udp/`.

assumes.text: The runner gives each check a fresh World that it uses for nothing else.
assumes.detail: FS checks reuse fixed names like "f", "d", "a" and "LOCK", and need an empty root.

systems.name: worldtest.Checks
systems.title: Core checks
systems.purpose: Check that channels, select, timers, locks, contexts and rand behave like Go.
systems.what: Checks is the core list. It asserts that the World's Chan, Select, Select2, Select3, timers, tickers, Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, contexts and Rand match the semantics of Go's built-ins and standard library. Rand is checked for in-range integers and for crypto-style byte reads via `CryptoRead` and `dst.CryptoReader`. Time checks measure in World time (`w.Now`, `w.Since`), so they hold under virtual time as well as real time.

interface.name: Checks
interface.doc: The core contract checks, run in listed order.

laws.text: Fails a World whose buffered Chan is not FIFO or whose Close semantics differ from Go's.
laws.detail: After Close, values already buffered can still be received, and a drained receive returns (0, false). Send or Close on a closed channel panics with Go's exact messages. A blocked receiver is woken with ok=false.

laws.text: Fails a Select that runs Default while a case is ready, or always picks the same ready case.
laws.detail: Over 200 selects with both cases ready, both must be chosen at least once, and the same holds for Select2. Nil channels must never be ready. Receiving from a closed channel must report ok=false, and OnDone must fire for a cancelled context.

laws.text: Fails Select2 or Select3 unless exactly the ready case fires, with its value.
laws.detail: Each send/receive direction is tried at each position, with one case ready. A select that hangs for a second of World time also fails.

laws.text: Fails timers that fire out of deadline order, or Stop that fails to prevent a fire.
laws.detail: This covers stopped timers, stopped AfterFuncs and stopped tickers. Reset must re-arm a timer that was stopped.

laws.text: Fails a Mutex or RWMutex that lets a writer overlap anyone, or never lets readers overlap.
Fails Once.Do if f runs more than once or Do returns before f finishes.
Fails a Cond where Signal doesn't wake exactly one waiter, or Broadcast doesn't wake all.
laws.detail: Wait must return holding L, and this covers a zero-value Cond with L set. A Signal or Broadcast made before anyone waits is lost.

laws.text: Fails World contexts whose cancel or timeout doesn't reach their children, standard-library children included.
laws.detail: Measured in World time from the context's creation, the timeout must not fire before its duration. Err must then be DeadlineExceeded. dst.Done must work on a context.WithValue wrapper.

laws.text: Fails Rand when IntN leaves its range, or crypto reads return short, zero or repeated bytes.
laws.detail: CryptoRead must fill 16 non-zero bytes without error. A following io.ReadFull from dst.CryptoReader(w) must succeed and give different bytes.

systems.name: worldtest.FSChecks
systems.title: Filesystem checks
systems.purpose: Check that w.FS() behaves like a POSIX filesystem rooted at the World.
systems.what: FSChecks runs against an empty `w.FS()`. They assert POSIX-like file semantics: open flags, append, sparse writes, truncation, directories, rename, removal, stat, closed handles, unlinked open files, file names as opened and hard links made with `dst.Link`. They also check that names cannot escape the root, that Sync and SyncDir succeed, and that `dst.LockFile` advisory locks are exclusive. Crash behaviour is out of scope.

interface.name: FSChecks
interface.doc: Filesystem, lock and hard-link contract checks on an empty FS.

laws.text: Fails an FS whose missing-path and existing-path errors don't match fs.ErrNotExist and fs.ErrExist.
laws.detail: Covered calls: Open, Mkdir, Rename, Remove and Link of missing paths, O_EXCL on an existing file, Mkdir of an existing directory, and Link onto an existing name.

laws.text: Fails an FS where writes past the end or Truncate growth don't zero-fill the gap.
Fails an FS where Rename doesn't atomically replace its target and drop the old name.
Fails an FS where an open file stops being readable after Remove.
Fails an FS that allows a path outside its root, such as "../escape".
Fails an FS where a closed handle can write or close again without an error.
laws.detail: Write after Close must return fs.ErrClosed.

laws.text: Fails an FS where FS.ReadDir isn't sorted by name, or Remove deletes a non-empty directory.
laws.detail: File.ReadDir order is allowed to be unspecified. RemoveAll of a missing path must succeed.

laws.text: Fails an FS whose File.Name isn't the name it was opened with.
laws.detail: As with os.File, Remove(f.Name()) must work on the same FS.

laws.text: Fails a LockFile that grants a held lock again, or not after unlock.
laws.detail: A second LockFile on a held name must fail with dst.ErrLocked, even within one process. LockFile must create its file, and locks on other names are independent.

laws.text: Fails a Link whose two names don't share data, or whose data dies with one name.
laws.detail: Appending through the link must be visible through the original, and after Remove of the original the link still reads the data while the old name is gone. Linking a directory must fail.

change.reason: New fs/link check adds a hard-link law and extends the ErrExist/ErrNotExist law to Link; evidence lines shifted by one.

systems.name: worldtest.NetChecks
systems.title: Network checks
systems.purpose: Check that w.Net() behaves like loopback TCP and UDP.
systems.what: NetChecks runs against `w.Net()` on localhost:0. Its TCP part checks stream semantics: echo, delivery in order, refused dials, read deadlines in World time, and EOF after the peer closes. Its UDP part uses `ListenPacket` and `Dial("udp")` and checks datagram semantics: echo with the right sender, whole-datagram boundaries, connected sockets, read deadlines, and Close unblocking a pending read.

interface.name: NetChecks
interface.doc: TCP and UDP contract checks over localhost.

laws.text: Fails a Net whose stream loses, reorders or duplicates the bytes written.
Fails a Net where Dial to a closed listener succeeds, or where Accept after Close isn't net.ErrClosed.
Fails a Net where a read past its deadline isn't a net.Error with Timeout() true.
laws.detail: The deadline is set from w.Now(), so it is World time.

laws.text: Fails a Net where reading after the peer closes isn't io.EOF, or writing after Close succeeds.
Fails a UDP socket that splits, merges or alters datagrams, or misreports an address.
laws.detail: Each ReadFrom must return exactly one datagram, whole (1, 100 and 1200 bytes are tried). It must name the sender's LocalAddr. A socket from Dial("udp") must report the server as RemoteAddr and get its echo back.

laws.text: Fails a UDP read past its deadline that isn't os.ErrDeadlineExceeded or returns early.
laws.detail: The 50ms deadline is measured in World time.

laws.text: Fails a PacketConn whose Close doesn't unblock a pending ReadFrom with net.ErrClosed.

systems.name: realworld.osFS
systems.title: Rooted filesystem
systems.purpose: Operating system filesystem confined to one directory via os.Root.
systems.what: `osFS` implements `dst.FS` over an `os.Root`, and also `dst.Linker` for hard links. The root is opened once, on first use, at the configured directory, or the current directory when that is empty. Every operation resolves names relative to that root, so code cannot reach files outside it. Opened files are wrapped as `rootFile` so they report the name they were opened with. On Unix, `LockFile` provides exclusive non-blocking advisory locks via flock(2). Durability and crash behaviour are whatever the OS provides.

laws.text: No FS call can read or change a name outside Options.Dir.
laws.detail: Absolute paths, `..` and escaping symlinks are rejected with an error. LockFile opens its file through the same root, and Link requires both names inside it.

laws.text: An empty Options.Dir roots the FS at the current directory.
If the root cannot be opened, every FS call returns that same error.
laws.detail: The root is opened once; the failure is cached, not retried. Link included.

laws.text: A failed OpenFile returns a nil dst.File, never a typed-nil *os.File.
A file from OpenFile reports Name() exactly as the name passed to OpenFile.
laws.detail: os.Root's files would report the root path joined to the name, and the root then rejects that path as escaping.

laws.text: LockFile on a file already locked fails at once with an error wrapping dst.ErrLocked.
laws.detail: The error is a *fs.PathError with Op "flock". LockFile never waits for the lock, and it closes the file it opened when locking fails.

laws.text: LockFile creates the lock file if it is missing.
Calling the returned unlock releases the lock and closes the file.
laws.detail: It returns the unlock error first, otherwise the close error.

assumes.text: os.Root rejects names that resolve outside its directory.
os.Root.Link behaves as os.Link for names inside the root.
flock(2) with LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB returns EWOULDBLOCK when another descriptor holds the lock.
assumes.detail: LockFile is built only on Unix (build tag unix).
